sources.title: Craftax: A Lightning-Fast Benchmark for Open-Ended Reinforcement Learning

sectionsRead: Section 3: Classic, Craftax mechanics, interface and evaluation
Sections 5–6; acknowledgements, impact statement and references
Appendices A–D: implementation, timing, resets, environment and interfaces
Appendices E–F: tuning, all achievement results, 10B and Classic
Appendix G: UED implementation, qualitative results and hyperparameters; all supplied tables through p. 34

Separate supplemental material availability has not been fully verified.
All eight supplied text chunks were read individually. Separate supplemental material availability has not been fully verified; no separate supplement was supplied.

Text extraction does not reconstruct figure images. Retained claims were checked against original PDF pages and six final crops. Figures 9–18 and Tables 2–3 were read through supplied text but not visually inspected.
No code, external project site or other external source was inspected; no experiments were reproduced.

Identity/version: the observed title exactly matches the catalog and all seven authors agree. The title page uses Matthew Jackson and Jakob Foerster where the catalog expands them to Matthew Thomas Jackson and Jakob Nicolaus Foerster. Catalog BibTeX includes Michael T. Matthews; this title page says Michael Matthews. No added author or title change was observed. The artifact identifies ICML 2024/PMLR 235; no finer revision date or revision chain was established.
The same PDF calls its 10B appendix condition Craftax-Extended. This label is retained without asserting a separately verified software edition.

synopsis: Craftax makes a procedurally generated survival game fast enough for billion-step reinforcement-learning studies. Its JAX implementation combines symbolic observations with accelerator-resident simulation and training. The harder environment exposes a gap between collecting easy rewards and exploring deeper floors: recurrent PPO helps, but the tested exploration and curriculum methods leave substantial challenges unsolved.

problem.text: Open-ended RL benchmarks trade complexity against affordable experimentation. The authors argue that slow survival games constrain research, while fast simple environments under-test exploration. Craftax separates a large-budget challenge from a small-budget sample-efficiency challenge.

contributions.text: Craftax-Classic reimplements Crafter in JAX; Craftax adds interconnected floors, richer combat, randomized potion meanings and attribute allocation. The contribution is an executable benchmark with baseline evidence.
Symbolic interfaces, compiled learning and optimistic resets make large experiments practical. Classic has documented differences from Crafter, so their scores are not strictly interchangeable.

inputs: Procedurally generated world state and an agent-selected discrete action
Agent observations: local map features plus inventory and player statistics
outputs: Updated simulator state, observation, reward and termination signal
Learned baseline policies and achievement/return measurements

steps.name: Generate and observe
steps.detail: Nine floors create related exploration contexts. A 9-by-11 local view encodes blocks, items, creatures and light, followed by inventory/statistics. Cells below light level 0.05 are masked. The reported flat symbolic observation sizes are 8268 for Craftax and 1345 for Classic.

steps.name: Act and receive feedback
steps.detail: Craftax has 43 discrete actions; Classic has 17. Unmet prerequisites turn an attempted action into a no-op that still advances time. First achievement completion earns its category reward, with additional damage/recovery terms.

steps.name: Compile collection and resets
steps.detail: Simulation and learning run on the accelerator. Fixed-capacity entity arrays permit compilation. Optimistic resets generate one fresh world per sixteen workers and allocate these to terminated episodes; overflow can duplicate initial states.

steps.name: Choose the training distribution
steps.detail: Ordinary training samples generated worlds. PLR prioritizes buffered levels by estimated regret; robust PLR updates only from replay. ACCEL adds mutations. UED separates short policy-learning rollouts from longer level-scoring trajectories.

training.text: Exploration baselines use four-layer, width-512 policy/value MLPs; PPO-RNN adds a GRU. The 1B PPO setup uses 1024 workers, 64-step rollouts, eight minibatches, four epochs and learning rate 0.0002 with annealing. Its sweep tunes parameters individually on one seed.

RND matches a fixed random target, ICM rewards world-model error, and E3B rewards episodic novelty. These auxiliary objectives change exploration during learning. The 1M random-search configuration instead uses 256 workers, 16-step rollouts and learning rate 0.0003.

inference.text: A policy maps observations, and recurrent state when present, to simulator actions; the next observation closes the loop. ICM is an intrinsic-reward baseline, not evidence of inference-time imagined-rollout planning or a unified future-and-action predictor.

The main challenges permit 1B or 1M symbolic-environment interactions. UED evaluates checkpoints on twenty fixed normally generated levels. This tests in-distribution procedural generalization, not transfer to novel game rules.

equations.explanation: Appendix C models X, simultaneous done flags, as binomial for 1024 workers with mean episode length 200. Generating 64 fresh states has a very small modeled overflow probability. This depends on the binomial assumption; it is not a guarantee under correlated terminations.

results.setting: One RTX 4090, i9-13900K, 32 GB RAM; each environment uses its best worker count.
results.metric: Environment steps per second; higher is faster
results.comparison: Crafter: 1,580 at 1024; Figure 2 reports approximately 169× and 257× speedups respectively.
results.interpretation: Measured pipeline throughput, not equal-architecture algorithmic speed. MineRL alone uses random actions; no timing uncertainty is tabulated.

results.setting: Craftax-Symbolic, 1B interactions, ten seeds; one-standard-error shading.
results.metric: Reward as percentage of the stated maximum 226
results.value: PPO-RNN approximately 15–16% at the endpoint, read from Figure 3.
results.comparison: PPO/ICM/RND near 12%; E3B near 11%. These are graph estimates, not exact table values.
results.interpretation: Memory improves reward, but Advanced and Very Advanced achievements remain unachieved. Dungeon entry improves without robust gnomish-mines exploration.

results.setting: Craftax-Symbolic, 1M interactions, ten seeds; one-standard-error shading.
results.value: All five methods finish near 2%, approximately read from Figure 6.
results.comparison: Little separation among PPO, PPO-RNN, ICM, E3B and RND.
results.interpretation: Short-budget results mostly measure basic achievement acquisition rather than deeper exploration.

results.setting: Appendix F.2 condition, PPO-RNN, 10B interactions, four seeds.
results.value: Approximately 17% reward in Figure 22; no gnomish-mines entry in Figure 21.
results.comparison: Modest progress beyond the separate 1B experiment; seed counts differ.
results.interpretation: More interactions do not establish deeper exploration. The learning-rate explanation for late gains is an author hypothesis.

results.setting: Appendix F.3, 1B interactions, ten seeds; plots identify PPO-RNN.
results.value: About 90%, consistent with the rounded headline; Figure 23 stays below full completion.
results.comparison: Diamonds and eating plants remain unreliable. The introduction calls the 51-minute run PPO; the appendix labels it PPO-RNN.
results.interpretation: Near-saturation motivates Craftax; universal achievement completion and an unambiguous feedforward-PPO result are not established.

results.setting: 1B training interactions; twenty fixed normally generated evaluation levels; ten runs.
results.metric: Evaluation reward as percentage of maximum
results.value: PLR ranks highest; unrestricted-swap ACCEL ranks lowest in Figure 7.
results.comparison: DR remains competitive. Swapping curricula perform better on replay than normally generated levels.
results.interpretation: Curriculum return cannot substitute for evaluation return. Equal interactions do not equalize gradient updates or hyperparameters.

limitations.text: Symbolic observations remove much visual representation learning. These experiments do not establish pixel-based control, physical execution or indefinite improvement beyond the finite achievement inventory.

Recurrent PPO trades overworld zombie rewards for underground achievements. E3B improves plant eating while lowering aggregate reward. Return alone therefore incompletely describes exploration coverage.

Discrepancies remain: the text says 65 achievements but Table 6 lists 67. Appendix D gives a 100,000-step cap, whereas G.1 says 4096 instead of a full 10,000. Figure 8 plots reward according to its axis/prose, although its caption says episode length.

The authors suggest intrinsic rewards distract from sufficiently dense extrinsic reward. The comparisons and limited 1B tuning do not isolate that explanation; UED comparisons also differ in update count and settings.

reproduction.text: Reconstruction requires matching Craftax, PureJaxRL/JaxUED, observation/reward settings and separate Tables 7–14 configurations. The paper links code and specifies hardware but does not pin an executable revision or package versions. Resolve achievement-count and episode-cap discrepancies before comparing scores.

Proposed check: compare full and optimistic resets with matched policies, logging overflow, duplicated worlds, throughput and achievements; correlate terminations to challenge the binomial assumption. This has not been run.

Proposed check: compare DR, PLR and robust PLR at equal interactions, then equal gradient-update budgets, with common evaluation levels and aligned learning rates. A disappearing advantage would implicate update exposure. This has not been run.

reasoning.text: The benchmark/simulator category and RL subcategory are supported. Architecture, prediction paradigm and WAM quadrant are not applicable: simulator baselines do not constitute a proposed One Model system. Physics simulation is not established by these grid-based game dynamics and merits separate catalog review. ICM prediction losses do not change the resource classification.

discussionQuestions: Would reward gains survive per-floor achievement reporting and equal-update curriculum controls?
Which dynamics require memory once policy capacity and training budget are controlled?

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title, author block, affiliation and proceedings footnotes
evidence.detail: The matching title credits Michael Matthews, Michael Beukman, Benjamin Ellis, Mikayel Samvelyan, Matthew Jackson, Samuel Coward and Jakob Foerster. Affiliations are University of Oxford and University College London. The artifact identifies ICML 2024, PMLR 235; no finer revision identifier is printed here.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 1–3, Abstract, Sections 1, 2.1–2.2 and 3.1
evidence.detail: A JAX rewrite of Crafter and a harder Craftax benchmark combine accelerator-based collection and training. Symbolic observations prioritize exploration research over pixel representation learning.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 3–4, Section 3.2, Multiple Floors through Boss Floor
evidence.detail: Nine procedurally generated floors connected by ladders, expanded combat, per-episode potion-effect permutations, experience allocation and a final boss are intended to challenge exploration, memory and adaptation.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 4–5, Section 3.3; p. 17, Appendix D.4–D.5; p. 22, Figure 25; pp. 30–31, Tables 4–5
evidence.detail: Reported symbolic observation sizes are 1345 for Classic and 8268 for Craftax; action counts are 17 and 43. Craftax observes a 9-by-11 map area, categorical block/item/creature features, light and inventory. Cells below light 0.05 are masked. Unsupported actions consume a timestep as no-ops. Figure 25 depicts optional pixel interfaces.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Section 3.3, Reward; p. 6, Section 4.3; p. 32, Table 6
evidence.detail: Achievements pay once per episode, with category rewards 1/3/5/8 and damage/recovery terms of minus/plus 0.1 per point. Section 3.3 states 65 achievements, but Table 6 lists IDs 0–66. Section 4.3 uses maximum achievement reward 226.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Section 3.4 and Figure 3 caption; p. 7, Figure 6 caption
evidence.detail: Craftax-1B and Craftax-1M use symbolic observations and one billion or one million interactions. Exploration curves use ten seeds with one-standard-error shading.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 5–6, Section 4.1; p. 33, Tables 8–10
evidence.detail: PureJaxRL PPO uses four-layer width-512 policy/value MLPs; PPO-RNN adds a GRU. RND distills a random network; ICM uses world-model error as intrinsic reward; E3B rewards episodic novelty. Table 8 lists forward and inverse model losses. No inference-time imagined-rollout planner is introduced.

evidence.location: PDF p. 17, Appendix E.1–E.2; pp. 33–34, Tables 7–13
evidence.detail: The 1B PPO sweep tunes parameters individually on one seed. Selected settings include 1024 workers, 64 steps, eight minibatches, four epochs and learning rate 0.0002. PPO-RNN inherits PPO settings and width-sized recurrent state. The 1M random-search baseline uses 256 workers, 16 steps and learning rate 0.0003. Both anneal learning rate.

evidence.location: PDF p. 12, Appendix A.1–A.2
evidence.detail: Classic uses fixed creature/plant capacities and inactive-entity masks, and replaces Crafter Simplex noise with Perlin noise.

evidence.location: PDF p. 12, Appendix B; p. 14, Table 1, all rows; p. 2, Figure 2 caption
evidence.detail: Best-case throughput is 405618 steps/s for Classic and 266961 for Craftax at 4096 workers, versus 1580 for Crafter at 1024. Hardware is one RTX 4090 with 24 GB VRAM, i9-13900K and 32 GB RAM. Learning pipelines are measured, except MineRL uses random actions; implementations and architectures are not identical.

evidence.location: PDF p. 14, Appendix C
evidence.detail: Generate M fresh worlds for N workers with M much smaller than N, using one world per sixteen workers. Overflow can duplicate initial states. The illustrative binomial calculation uses 1024 workers, mean episode length 200 and 64 new states; an approximately twofold speedup is reported.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Figure 3; p. 6, Figure 4 and Section 4.3
evidence.detail: At 1B interactions PPO-RNN is near 15–16% of maximum reward, PPO/ICM/RND near 12%, and E3B near 11%. These are approximate visual readings, not tabulated endpoints. Figure 4 shows no progress in Advanced or Very Advanced categories.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 6–7, Section 4.3 and Figure 5; p. 18, Figure 19
evidence.detail: PPO-RNN enters the dungeon more frequently while zombie completion declines, interpreted by the authors as a tradeoff between overworld and underground rewards. Gnomish-mines entry remains rare. E3B improves EAT_PLANT despite lower overall reward. Figure 5 uses a different palette from Figure 3.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Section 4.4 and Figure 6; p. 19, Figure 20
evidence.detail: The 1M methods have similar returns, approximately 2% of maximum by visual reading. Achievement curves show mostly basic progress and isolated dungeon entries.

evidence.location: PDF p. 19, Appendix F.2; p. 20, Figure 21; p. 21, Figure 22
evidence.detail: The 10B appendix condition is called Craftax-Extended. Four PPO-RNN seeds reach roughly 17% reward, with no gnomish-mines entry. The authors associate late acceleration with the learning-rate schedule.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 1–2, Abstract and Introduction; p. 21, Appendix F.3 and Figure 23; p. 22, Figure 24
evidence.detail: The headline describes about 90% of optimal Classic reward and a 51-minute PPO run. Appendix F.3 and Figures 23–24 explicitly identify PPO-RNN, ten seeds and 1B interactions. Diamonds and eating plants remain unreliable; all achievements are not consistently completed.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section 4.2; p. 7, Section 4.5 mutation operators
evidence.detail: PLR curates levels by estimated regret; robust PLR trains only on replay. ACCEL also mutates levels through noise, unrestricted swaps or restricted swaps. Domain randomization samples normally generated levels.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 7–8, Section 4.5 and Figure 7; p. 26, Figure 34
evidence.detail: UED evaluates checkpoints on twenty fixed normally generated levels over ten runs. PLR has the highest reward and unrestricted-swap ACCEL the lowest. Robust PLR performs fewer updates at equal interactions. Evaluation uses the normal generator, not a separately shifted test distribution.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Distribution Shift and Figure 8; pp. 24–25, Figures 32–33
evidence.detail: Swapping curricula show higher replay reward than reward on normally generated levels, with achievement differences such as diamond collection. Figure 8 has a Reward (% of Max) axis and average-return prose, but an average-episode-length caption. This discrepancy remains unresolved.

evidence.location: PDF p. 22, Appendix G.1; p. 23, Appendix G.2–G.3 and Figures 26–31; p. 27, Table 14
evidence.detail: UED separates short learning rollouts from longer regret scoring. Table 14 gives 64 inner and 64 outer rollout steps, 1024 environments, and replay rates 0.5 for PLR/ACCEL and 0.8 for robust PLR. ACCEL updates on DR but not mutated levels. Learning rates and mutation counts differ between algorithms.

evidence.location: PDF p. 14, opening of Appendix D; p. 22, final sentence of Appendix G.1
evidence.detail: Appendix D states a maximum episode length of 100000. Appendix G.1 says UED uses 4096 instead of a full 10000. The descriptions of the full horizon conflict.

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, code footnote; p. 12, Appendix B; p. 17, Appendix E; p. 27, Table 14; pp. 33–34, Tables 7–13
evidence.detail: The paper provides a code link, hardware and hyperparameters, but no pinned executable revision or package-version environment in these reproducibility details.
